The coefficient of ϵk\epsilon^{k}ϵk in det⁡(I+ϵA)\det(I+\epsilon A)det(I+ϵA) is the sum of the principal k×kk\times kk×k minors, starting at 111, then trA\mathrm{tr}AtrA, and ending at det⁡A\det AdetA. Trace and determinant are the first and last members of one family, and it is the family Chapter 0.5 will identify with the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial.

How good is first order? At ϵ=0.01\epsilon=0.01ϵ=0.01 the exact value is 1.0590691.0590691.059069, against the linear estimate 1+6ϵ=1.061+6\epsilon=1.061+6ϵ=1.06. That is an error of −9.31×10−4-9.31\times10^{-4}−9.31×10−4, where the quadratic term alone predicts −9ϵ2=−9.00×10−4-9\epsilon^{2}=-9.00\times10^{-4}−9ϵ2=−9.00×10−4. Agreement to two figures, with the small residue supplied by the cubic term, which is exactly the behaviour the O(ϵ2)O(\epsilon^{2})O(ϵ2) notation promises. This is Chapter 0.1's linearisation applied to a function of nine variables, and it behaves exactly as advertised.

9 · Your turn

Problem 1 · a two-dimensional space with no arrows in it

Show that the set of solutions of y′′+ω2y=0y''+\omega^{2}y=0y′′+ω2y=0 (with ω≠0\omega\neq0ω=0 fixed) is a vector space, that {cos⁡ωt, sin⁡ωt}\{\cos\omega t,\ \sin\omega t\}{cosωt, sinωt} is a basis for it, and hence that its dimension is 222. Then say what the "two arbitrary constants" of your first differential-equations course actually are.

Solution

Vector space. This is (0.4.3) with p=0p=0p=0, q=ω2q=\omega^{2}q=ω2: if y1,y2y_{1},y_{2}y1​,y2​ are solutions then (ay1+by2)′′+ω2(ay1+by2)=a(y1′′+ω2y1)+b(y2′′+ω2y2)=0(ay_{1}+by_{2})''+\omega^{2}(ay_{1}+by_{2}) = a(y_{1}''+\omega^{2}y_{1}) + b(y_{2}''+\omega^{2}y_{2}) = 0(ay1​+by2​)′′+ω2(ay1​+by2​)=a(y1′′​+ω2y1​)+b(y2′′​+ω2y2​)=0. The zero function is a solution, so the set is nonempty and closed under both operations. ✓

Both candidates are solutions. d2dt2cos⁡ωt=−ω2cos⁡ωt\dv{^{2}}{t^{2}}\cos\omega t = -\omega^{2}\cos\omega tdt2d2​cosωt=−ω2cosωt and likewise for sin⁡\sinsin (Chapter 0.1). ✓

Independent. Suppose acos⁡ωt+bsin⁡ωt=0a\cos\omega t + b\sin\omega t = 0acosωt+bsinωt=0 for all ttt. Put t=0t=0t=0: a=0a=0a=0. Differentiate and put t=0t=0t=0: bω=0b\omega = 0bω=0, and ω≠0\omega\neq0ω=0, so b=0b=0b=0. ✓

Spanning, which is the only part with any content. Let yyy be any solution. Set c1=y(0)c_{1}=y(0)c1​=y(0) and c2=y′(0)/ωc_{2}=y'(0)/\omegac2​=y′(0)/ω, and define u=y−c1cos⁡ωt−c2sin⁡ωtu = y - c_{1}\cos\omega t - c_{2}\sin\omega tu=y−c1​cosωt−c2​sinωt. Then uuu solves the same equation, since it is a combination of solutions, and it satisfies u(0)=0u(0)=0u(0)=0 and u′(0)=0u'(0)=0u′(0)=0. Now consider

E(t)  ≡  (u′)2+ω2u2,E′=2u′u′′+2ω2uu′=2u′(u′′+ω2u)=0. E(t) \;\equiv\; \big(u'\big)^{2} + \omega^{2}u^{2}, \qquad E' = 2u'u'' + 2\omega^{2}uu' = 2u'\big(u''+\omega^{2}u\big) = 0. E(t)≡(u′)2+ω2u2,E′=2u′u′′+2ω2uu′=2u′(u′′+ω2u)=0.

So EEE is constant, and E(0)=0E(0)=0E(0)=0. Both terms of EEE are non-negative and sum to zero, so each is zero for every ttt. In particular u≡0u\equiv0u≡0, and y=c1cos⁡ωt+c2sin⁡ωty = c_{1}\cos\omega t + c_{2}\sin\omega ty=c1​cosωt+c2​sinωt. ✓ (That EEE is the energy of a harmonic oscillator is not an accident, and Chapter 0.8 will make a habit of this trick.)

Hence the solution set has a basis with two elements and dimension 222.

The constants. They are coordinates. Specifying a solution means specifying a vector in a two-dimensional space, which takes exactly two numbers.

The familiar alternative form y=Ccos⁡(ωt−φ)y = C\cos(\omega t-\varphi)y=Ccos(ωt−φ) is not a different solution set. It is a different parametrisation of the same plane. Expanding it gives Ccos⁡φcos⁡ωt+Csin⁡φsin⁡ωtC\cos\varphi\cos\omega t + C\sin\varphi\sin\omega tCcosφcosωt+Csinφsinωt, so (c1,c2)=(Ccos⁡φ,Csin⁡φ)(c_{1},c_{2}) = (C\cos\varphi, C\sin\varphi)(c1​,c2​)=(Ccosφ,Csinφ), which is polar coordinates on the same two-dimensional space. Amplitude-and-phase versus sine-and-cosine is a change of description, and the physics is in neither.

Problem 2 · differentiation as a matrix, and why integration needs a +C+C+C

Let DDD be the derivative operator on P3P_{3}P3​, the polynomials of degree ≤3\le3≤3, with basis {1, x, x2, x3}\{1,\ x,\ x^{2},\ x^{3}\}{1, x, x2, x3}. Write down its matrix. Compute det⁡D\det DdetD and tr D\mathrm{tr}\,DtrD, and interpret both.

Solution

Apply (0.4.9): the jjj-th column is the image of the jjj-th basis vector, written in coordinates. With e1=1, e2=x, e3=x2, e4=x3e_{1}=1,\ e_{2}=x,\ e_{3}=x^{2},\ e_{4}=x^{3}e1​=1, e2​=x, e3​=x2, e4​=x3:

D(1)=0,D(x)=1=e1,D(x2)=2x=2e2,D(x3)=3x2=3e3, D(1)=0, \qquad D(x)=1=e_{1}, \qquad D(x^{2})=2x=2e_{2}, \qquad D(x^{3})=3x^{2}=3e_{3}, D(1)=0,D(x)=1=e1​,D(x2)=2x=2e2​,D(x3)=3x2=3e3​, soD=(0100002000030000). \text{so}\qquad D = \begin{pmatrix}0&1&0&0\\ 0&0&2&0\\ 0&0&0&3\\ 0&0&0&0\end{pmatrix}. soD=​0000​1000​0200​0030​​.

Determinant. The first column is entirely zero, so by multilinearity (D1) the determinant is linear in that column and D(…,0,… )=0D(\dots,0,\dots)=0D(…,0,…)=0. Hence det⁡D=0\det D = 0detD=0. Equivalently, the matrix is triangular with zero diagonal.

By (0.4.25) the operator is not invertible, and §5 says what that means concretely. It destroys information, and here you can name the information exactly. DDD kills every constant, so 111 and 1+71+71+7 and 1−π1-\pi1−π all have the same image, and no operation can tell them apart afterwards.

That is the constant of integration. The +C+C+C is not a bookkeeping nicety. It is the statement that det⁡D=0\det D=0detD=0, and that antidifferentiation is therefore not a function but a one-parameter family.

Here is the geometry. The image of DDD is P2P_{2}P2​, of dimension 333, so a four-dimensional space has been flattened onto a three-dimensional one. The unit hypercube of P3P_{3}P3​ has been crushed to zero four-volume, which is exactly the collapse the interactive shows in two dimensions.

Trace. tr D=0+0+0+0=0\mathrm{tr}\,D = 0+0+0+0 = 0trD=0+0+0+0=0. That is consistent with (0.4.29), because det⁡(I+ϵD)=1\det(I+\epsilon D) = 1det(I+ϵD)=1 exactly, since I+ϵDI+\epsilon DI+ϵD is triangular with 111s on the diagonal, and the linear term ϵ trD\epsilon\,\mathrm{tr}DϵtrD is indeed zero.

Nudging the identity in the direction of "differentiate a bit" changes no volume at all to first order. That is reassuring, since DDD is nilpotent, meaning D4=0D^{4}=0D4=0: differentiate a cubic four times and nothing is left. Nilpotent operators always have zero trace.

Problem 3 · how far does the cyclic property go?

Prove tr(AB)=tr(BA)\mathrm{tr}(AB)=\mathrm{tr}(BA)tr(AB)=tr(BA) for all square A,BA,BA,B of the same size. Then show tr(ABC)=tr(BCA)\mathrm{tr}(ABC)=\mathrm{tr}(BCA)tr(ABC)=tr(BCA) follows immediately, but that tr(ABC)=tr(ACB)\mathrm{tr}(ABC)=\mathrm{tr}(ACB)tr(ABC)=tr(ACB) is false in general. Give an explicit 2×22\times22×2 counterexample.

Solution

Two factors. This is (0.4.27): tr(AB)=∑i,jAijBji=∑j,iBjiAij=tr(BA)\mathrm{tr}(AB)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ji}=\sum_{j,i}B_{ji}A_{ij}=\mathrm{tr}(BA)tr(AB)=∑i,j​Aij​Bji​=∑j,i​Bji​Aij​=tr(BA), using only commutativity of the scalars and the fact that a finite double sum may be reordered.

Three factors, cyclically. Apply the two-factor result with X=ABX=ABX=AB and Y=CY=CY=C:

tr(ABC)=tr((AB)C)=tr(C(AB))=tr(CAB), \mathrm{tr}(ABC) = \mathrm{tr}\big((AB)C\big) = \mathrm{tr}\big(C(AB)\big) = \mathrm{tr}(CAB), tr(ABC)=tr((AB)C)=tr(C(AB))=tr(CAB),

and once more with X=AX=AX=A, Y=BCY=BCY=BC gives tr(ABC)=tr(BCA)\mathrm{tr}(ABC)=\mathrm{tr}(BCA)tr(ABC)=tr(BCA). So the three cyclic rotations ABCABCABC, BCABCABCA, CABCABCAB all agree.

The other three orderings need not. Take

A=(0100),B=(0010),C=(1000). A = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad B = \begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad C = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}. A=(00​10​),B=(01​00​),C=(10​00​).

Then AB=(1000)AB = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}AB=(10​00​), so ABC=(1000)ABC = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}ABC=(10​00​) and tr(ABC)=1\mathrm{tr}(ABC)=1tr(ABC)=1. But AC=(0100)(1000)=0AC = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix} = 0AC=(00​10​)(10​00​)=0, so ACB=0ACB = 0ACB=0 and tr(ACB)=0≠1\mathrm{tr}(ACB) = 0 \neq 1tr(ACB)=0=1. ✓

The moral. The trace is invariant under cyclic permutation and not under arbitrary permutation. Cycling is the only rearrangement you can reach by repeatedly moving the last factor to the front, and that is all tr(XY)=tr(YX)\mathrm{tr}(XY)=\mathrm{tr}(YX)tr(XY)=tr(YX) licenses. Anyone who forgets this and "simplifies" tr(ABC)\mathrm{tr}(ABC)tr(ABC) to tr(ACB)\mathrm{tr}(ACB)tr(ACB) has assumed BC=CBBC=CBBC=CB.

This is not an idle warning. In Chapter 5.9 you will evaluate traces of products of gamma matrices, which anticommute rather than commute. The cyclic property is what makes those traces computable, and the absence of the non-cyclic property is what makes them interesting.

Problem 4 · every entry changes, two numbers do not

Let TTT have matrix A=(2134)A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\3&4\end{pmatrix}A=(23​14​) in the standard basis. Change to the basis e1′=e1+e2e'_{1}=e_{1}+e_{2}e1′​=e1​+e2​, e2′=2e1+3e2e'_{2}=2e_{1}+3e_{2}e2′​=2e1​+3e2​. Compute A′=P−1APA'=P^{-1}APA′=P−1AP, verify directly from (0.4.17) that A′A'A′ really is the matrix of the same map, and check the determinant and trace.

Solution

By (0.4.14) the columns of PPP are the new basis vectors in old coordinates, so P=(1213)P = \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix}P=(11​23​), with det⁡P=1\det P = 1detP=1. The 2×22\times22×2 inverse, which you can verify by multiplying out, is P−1=(3−2−11)P^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}3&-2\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}P−1=(3−1​−21​). Then

AP=(2134)(1213)=(37718),A′=P−1(AP)=(−5−15411). AP = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3&7\\7&18\end{pmatrix}, \qquad A' = P^{-1}(AP) = \begin{pmatrix}-5&-15\\ 4&11\end{pmatrix}. AP=(23​14​)(11​23​)=(37​718​),A′=P−1(AP)=(−54​−1511​).

Direct check. (0.4.17) says that column 111 of A′A'A′ should be the coordinates of T(e1′)T(e'_{1})T(e1′​) in the new basis. Compute the left side, which is T(e1′)=A(11)=(37)T(e'_{1}) = A\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\7\end{pmatrix}T(e1′​)=A(11​)=(37​). Now the right side, which is −5e1′+4e2′=−5(11)+4(23)=(37)-5e'_{1}+4e'_{2} = -5\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}+4\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\7\end{pmatrix}−5e1′​+4e2′​=−5(11​)+4(23​)=(37​). ✓ Same vector. Likewise T(e2′)=A(23)=(718)T(e'_{2}) = A\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}7\\18\end{pmatrix}T(e2′​)=A(23​)=(718​) and −15e1′+11e2′=(−15+22−15+33)=(718)-15e'_{1}+11e'_{2} = \begin{pmatrix}-15+22\\ -15+33\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}7\\18\end{pmatrix}−15e1′​+11e2′​=(−15+22−15+33​)=(718​). ✓

Invariants.

trA=2+4=6,trA′=−5+11=6;det⁡A=8−3=5,det⁡A′=−55+60=5. \mathrm{tr}A = 2+4 = 6, \qquad \mathrm{tr}A' = -5+11 = 6; \qquad \det A = 8-3 = 5, \qquad \det A' = -55+60 = 5. trA=2+4=6,trA′=−5+11=6;detA=8−3=5,detA′=−55+60=5.

Not one of the four entries stayed where it was. The numbers 2,1,3,42,1,3,42,1,3,4 became −5,−15,4,11-5,-15,4,11−5,−15,4,11, and only the 444 so much as reappears, in a different slot. Yet the trace and the determinant are untouched, exactly as (0.4.24) and (0.4.28) guarantee.

If you were handed only A′A'A′ and asked "what does this map do to areas?", you would answer 555, the same answer as from AAA, because that question is about the map. If you were asked "what is the top-left entry?", you would be answering a question about the basis.

This is the entire chapter in four numbers.

The brick you just laid

You have the vector space defined by what you may do to its elements rather than by what they look like, so that functions, polynomials, matrices, solutions of differential equations and quantum states are all vectors and all obey the same theorems.

You have coordinates, proved unique, together with the discipline of never confusing the vector with its coordinate list.

You have matrix multiplication derived from composition of maps, including why the shapes must match, why it is associative for free, and why it does not commute.

You have the change-of-basis law A′=P−1APA'=P^{-1}APA′=P−1AP, and the distinction between what changes with the description and what does not.

You have the determinant as signed volume, from three properties rather than a formula, with det⁡(AB)=det⁡Adet⁡B\det(AB)=\det A\det Bdet(AB)=detAdetB as a one-line statement that scaling factors multiply, and det⁡=0\det=0det=0 as the destruction of information.

And you have the trace: cyclic, basis independent, and, in the identity worth the whole chapter, the first-order determinant det⁡(I+ϵA)=1+ϵ trA+O(ϵ2)\det(I+\epsilon A)=1+\epsilon\,\mathrm{tr}A+O(\epsilon^{2})det(I+ϵA)=1+ϵtrA+O(ϵ2).

Where this gets spent. Basis and coordinates → Chapter 2.4 (a tensor is defined by its transformation law, which is §4) and Chapter 3.2 (physics must not depend on coordinates). Composition of linear maps → Chapter 0.6, where the chain rule becomes a product of Jacobian matrices and is the same statement as (0.4.13). Determinant → Chapter 0.6 again (the Jacobian determinant in a change of variables is precisely "the factor by which volume is multiplied") and Chapter 3.5, where −g\sqrt{-g}−g​, the square root of a determinant, is what makes an integral over curved spacetime mean anything. Trace → Chapter 0.7 (divergence is the trace of the Jacobian), Chapter 1.3 (Liouville's theorem is tr=0\mathrm{tr}=0tr=0), and Chapter 6.1 (the generators of SU(NNN) are traceless because det⁡eA=etrA\det\ee^{A}=\ee^{\mathrm{tr}A}deteA=etrA, which is why there are eight gluons). Non-commutativity → Chapter 4.9 (uncertainty), Chapter 3.4 (curvature), Chapter 6.4 (Yang–Mills self-interaction). Complex scalars → Chapter 4.2, where the existence of eigenvalues is the existence of measurable values.

Next, Chapter 0.5 asks the follow-up question this chapter has been setting up. Given an operator, can we find a basis in which its matrix is as simple as possible? For a large and physically crucial class of operators the answer is yes, and the simple form is diagonal. The diagonal entries are the eigenvalues that this chapter has twice promised.
